clinicalPearls: Part of the exstrophy-epispadias complex, ranging in severity from isolated epispadias through classic bladder exstrophy to cloacal exstrophy
Presents at birth with an open, everted bladder plate exposed on the lower abdominal wall through a midline infra-umbilical defect
Associated with pubic diastasis (separation of the symphysis pubis) and, in males, epispadias with a dorsally opened, short penis
The upper urinary tracts are usually initially normal, but continence and cosmesis depend on reconstruction
More common in males than females
Management is staged or single-stage surgical reconstruction aimed at secure abdominal/bladder closure, epispadias repair, and eventual continence, often with bladder neck reconstruction
Long-term surveillance is needed for reflux, upper-tract deterioration, continence, sexual function, and an increased lifetime risk of bladder malignancy
reference.pathophysiology: Bladder exstrophy arises from a developmental failure during formation of the lower abdominal wall and anterior bladder wall. An abnormally developed or prematurely ruptured cloacal membrane is thought to prevent medial migration of mesenchyme, so the structures that should form the anterior abdominal wall, anterior bladder, and anterior urethra fail to close in the midline. The bladder is left open and everted, the pubic bones are separated, and the genitalia are epispadic. The severity depends on the timing and extent of the developmental disturbance, giving the spectrum of the exstrophy-epispadias complex.
additionalDifferentials: Cloacal exstrophy (more severe, with bowel involvement)
Omphalocele or gastroschisis affecting the abdominal wall
additionalInvestigations: Renal and bladder ultrasound to document upper-tract anatomy and bladder plate size
Micturating cystourethrogram (MCUG) after closure to assess reflux
MAG3 renogram to monitor differential function and drainage
Pelvic imaging to characterise pubic diastasis for surgical planning
Examination and imaging for associated genital and skeletal anomalies
redFlags: Upper-tract dilatation or deteriorating renal function on follow-up
Recurrent urinary tract infection with high-grade reflux after closure
Wound dehiscence or bladder prolapse after primary closure
New bladder mass or haematuria in adulthood raising concern for malignancy
reference.prognosis: With modern staged or single-stage reconstruction most children can achieve satisfactory continence and preservation of renal function, though multiple operations are common and long-term risks include reflux, sexual and fertility issues, and an elevated risk of bladder cancer requiring lifelong follow-up.
pitfalls: Delaying or mishandling initial closure, jeopardising later continence and upper-tract preservation
Failing to recognise associated pubic diastasis and its implications for pelvic reconstruction
Neglecting long-term cancer surveillance of reconstructed or augmented bladders
Underestimating the psychosocial, sexual, and fertility impact into adulthood
management: Surgical reconstruction, staged or single-stage, to achieve secure abdominal-wall and anterior bladder closure as the foundation of management
Epispadias repair and, subsequently, bladder neck reconstruction to achieve urinary continence and acceptable genital reconstruction
Pelvic osteotomy to approximate the separated pubic symphysis and support a tension-free closure
Protect the upper urinary tracts, with post-closure micturating cystourethrography for vesicoureteric reflux and its management
Long-term surveillance of renal function, continence, sexual and fertility outcomes and the elevated risk of bladder cancer
Coordinate lifelong care through a specialist paediatric urology and reconstructive team
